Construction CFO Training Curriculum - Months 5-8

Comprehensive Textbook Manuscript

Month 5: General Ledger, Chart of Accounts, and Journal Entries

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 5, you will:

  • Design comprehensive chart of accounts tailored for construction operations
  • Master the integration between general ledger accounts and job costing systems
  • Execute standard journal entries for construction operations with precision
  • Implement advanced month-end closing procedures and controls
  • Establish robust internal controls and documentation requirements

Overview

The general ledger serves as the foundation of construction accounting, but unlike other industries, construction requires specialized account structures that accommodate project-based operations, work-in-progress tracking, and complex cost allocation. This month builds your expertise in designing, implementing, and managing sophisticated general ledger systems that support both financial reporting and operational decision-making.

Week 1: Construction-Specific Chart of Accounts Design

The Strategic Foundation of Construction Accounting

The chart of accounts is not merely a list of accounts—it's the architectural blueprint of your financial system. In construction, this blueprint must accommodate unique industry characteristics while maintaining the flexibility to scale with business growth.

Core Principles of Construction Chart of Accounts

1. Project Integration Every account must seamlessly integrate with job costing systems. Consider this example:

Account 5100 - Direct Labor

  • Must track labor by project
  • Should accommodate phase/cost code breakdowns
  • Must integrate with payroll systems
  • Should support equipment hour allocation

2. Multi-Dimensional Flexibility Modern construction accounting requires multi-dimensional tracking:

Dimension Examples:

  • Entity: Multiple legal entities or divisions
  • Project: Individual jobs or contracts
  • Cost Code: CSI-based cost categorization
  • Phase: Construction sequence tracking
  • Location: Geographic or site-specific

Comprehensive Account Structure Framework

ASSETS (1000-1999)

Current Assets (1000-1499)

Cash and Cash Equivalents (1000-1099)

1000 - Operating Cash - Primary checking account

1010 - Payroll Cash - Dedicated payroll account

1020 - Project Cash - Customer deposits and escrows

1025 - Retainage Cash - Restricted cash for retainage

1030 - Money Market - Short-term liquid investments

1040 - Petty Cash - Job site cash funds

1050 - Restricted Cash - Letter of credit deposits

Why This Structure Matters: Segregating cash by purpose provides better cash flow management and reduces reconciliation complexity. The CFO needs immediate visibility into available operating cash versus restricted funds.

Accounts Receivable (1100-1199)

1100 - Accounts Receivable - Trade (current billings)

1110 - Accounts Receivable - Retainage (5-10% withheld)

1115 - Accounts Receivable - Long-term Retainage (due >1 year)

1120 - Unbilled Receivables - Earned but not billed

1125 - Notes Receivable - Customer financing arrangements

1130 - Employee Advances - Travel and expense advances

1140 - Other Receivables - Claims, insurance, etc.

1150 - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts - Contra asset

Critical CFO Insight: Retainage timing drives cash flow. Separate current (due within 1 year) from long-term retainage for accurate liquidity analysis.

Work-in-Progress and Inventory (1200-1399)

1200 - Raw Materials Inventory - Lumber, steel, concrete

1210 - Supplies Inventory - Small tools, safety equipment

1220 - Work in Process - Job cost accumulation

1250 - Costs in Excess of Billings - WIP asset (overbilled work)

1260 - Contract Assets - ASC 606 contract assets

1300 - Land Held for Development - Future projects

1310 - Construction in Progress - Assets for own use

The WIP Connection: Account 1250 is crucial for revenue recognition. When costs incurred plus recognized profit exceed customer billings, this account captures the asset representing work performed but not yet billed.

LIABILITIES (2000-2999)

Current Liabilities (2000-2499)

Trade Payables (2000-2099)

2000 - Accounts Payable - Trade vendors

2010 - Accounts Payable - Subcontractors

2020 - Retainage Payable - Amounts withheld from subs

2025 - Contract Retainage Payable - Customer retainage held

2030 - Accrued Trade Payables - Goods received, not invoiced

Customer-Related Liabilities (2200-2299)

2200 - Billings in Excess of Costs - WIP liability (underbilled work)

2210 - Customer Deposits - Advance payments received

2215 - Contract Liabilities - ASC 606 contract liabilities

2220 - Warranty Reserve - Future warranty obligations

2230 - Contract Completion Reserve - Punch list items

REVENUE (4000-4999)

Construction Revenue by Type (4000-4499)

4000 - Single-Family Construction Revenue

4100 - Multifamily Construction Revenue

4200 - Commercial Construction Revenue

4300 - Renovation/Remodel Revenue

4400 - Change Order Revenue - Contract modifications

4450 - Claims Revenue - Disputed/extra work

4500 - Service Revenue - Maintenance, warranty

Revenue Recognition Note: Under ASC 606, all construction revenue should use percentage-of-completion method. Separate revenue types enable margin analysis and project profitability tracking.

COST OF SALES (5000-5999)

Direct Construction Costs by Type (5000-5399)

5000 - Direct Materials - Single Family

5010 - Direct Materials - Multifamily

5020 - Direct Materials - Commercial

5100 - Direct Labor - Single Family

5110 - Direct Labor - Multifamily

5120 - Direct Labor - Commercial

5200 - Subcontractors - Single Family

5210 - Subcontractors - Multifamily

5220 - Subcontractors - Commercial

5300 - Equipment Costs - Allocated to jobs

5310 - Fuel and Maintenance - Job-specific

5320 - Permits and Fees - Project-specific

Job Costing Integration Framework

The chart of accounts must integrate with job costing through dimensional coding:

Example Project Coding:

Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Project: SF-2024-001 (Single Family project)

Cost Code: 06110 (Rough Carpentry)

Phase: 03 (Framing)

Full Code: 5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

WIP Account Relationships

Critical Formula:

WIP Asset = (Costs Incurred + Gross Profit Recognized) - Progress Billings

When positive: Use Account 1250 (Costs in Excess of Billings) When negative: Use Account 2200 (Billings in Excess of Costs)

Technology Integration

Modern systems like Ledgerline Intacct support dimensional accounting:

Example Configuration:

Base Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Entity Dimension: CS (Construction Services)

Project Dimension: SF-2024-001

Cost Code Dimension: 06110

Phase Dimension: 03

Result: CS-5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

Week 2: Standard Journal Entries for Construction Operations

Master Framework for Construction Journal Entries

Construction accounting requires specialized journal entries that capture the unique nature of project-based operations, long-term contracts, and complex cost allocations.

Revenue Recognition Entries

Percentage-of-Completion Revenue Recognition

Scenario: Mountain View Homes Project

  • Contract Amount: $850,000
  • Costs Incurred to Date: $425,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $680,000
  • Previously Recognized Revenue: $250,000

Step 1: Calculate Percentage Complete

Percentage Complete = $425,000 ÷ $680,000 = 62.5%

Step 2: Calculate Total Revenue Earned

Total Revenue Earned = $850,000 × 62.5% = $531,250

Step 3: Calculate Current Period Revenue

Current Period Revenue = $531,250 - $250,000 = $281,250

Journal Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable $281,250

Cr. Construction Revenue - SF $281,250

(To recognize revenue based on percentage completion)

Progress Billing Entries

Scenario: Monthly progress billing with retainage

  • Work completed: $281,250
  • Customer retainage: 10%
  • Previous unpaid billings: $125,000

Progress Billing Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable - Trade $253,125

Dr. Accounts Receivable - Retainage $28,125

Cr. Billings on Construction Contracts $281,250

(Progress billing with 10% retainage withheld)

Collection Entry:

Dr. Cash $378,125

Cr. Accounts Receivable - Trade $378,125

(Collection of current and previous billings)

Change Order Revenue Recognition

Scenario: Customer-approved change order

  • Original contract: $850,000
  • Approved change order: $75,000
  • Change order work 60% complete

Change Order Revenue Entry:

Dr. Contract Asset - Change Orders $45,000

Cr. Change Order Revenue $45,000

(60% completion of $75,000 change order)

Cost Recording and Allocation Entries

Material Purchase and Allocation

Initial Purchase:

Dr. Raw Materials Inventory $125,000

Cr. Accounts Payable - Trade $125,000

(Lumber and concrete purchases)

Material Requisition to Projects:

Dr. Direct Materials - SF-001 $45,000

Dr. Direct Materials - MF-002 $55,000

Dr. Direct Materials - CC-003 $25,000

Cr. Raw Materials Inventory $125,000

(Allocate materials to specific projects)

Direct Labor Allocation

Comprehensive Payroll Entry

Weekly payroll processing:

Dr. Direct Labor - SF-001 $32,000

Dr. Direct Labor - MF-002 $48,000

Dr. Job Site Supervision $18,000

Dr. Administrative Salaries $12,000

Cr. Wages Payable $82,500

Cr. Federal Tax Withholding $16,500

Cr. State Tax Withholding $4,125

Cr. FICA Payable $6,875

Cr. Medicare Payable $1,608

Cr. 401k Employee Deferrals $2,750

Cr. Health Insurance Employee Share $4,640

(Payroll distribution across projects and overhead)

Payroll Tax Burden:

Dr. Direct Labor - SF-001 (Burden) $3,200

Dr. Direct Labor - MF-002 (Burden) $4,800

Dr. Job Site Supervision (Burden) $1,800

Dr. Payroll Tax Expense (Admin) $1,200

Cr. FICA Payable - Employer $6,875

Cr. Medicare Payable - Employer $1,608

Cr. FUTA Payable $660

Cr. SUTA Payable $1,857

(Employer payroll taxes by project and overhead)

Subcontractor Cost Recognition

Approved subcontractor invoice with retainage:

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $85,000

Cr. Accounts Payable - Subcontractors $76,500

Cr. Retainage Payable $8,500

(Plumbing subcontractor with 10% retainage)

Equipment Cost Allocation

Monthly Equipment Usage Allocation

Equipment depreciation and usage tracking:

Dr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $4,200

Dr. Equipment Costs - MF-002 $6,800

Dr. Equipment Costs - CC-003 $2,500

Dr. Equipment Depreciation - Office $1,500

Cr. Accumulated Depreciation - Equipment $15,000

(Allocate equipment depreciation based on usage)

Work-in-Progress Entries

WIP Asset Recognition

Project with costs exceeding billings:

  • Costs Incurred: $425,000
  • Revenue Recognized: $531,250
  • Progress Billings: $475,000
  • Gross Profit: $106,250
  • WIP Asset: ($425,000 + $106,250) - $475,000 = $56,250

WIP Asset Entry:

Dr. Costs in Excess of Billings $56,250

Cr. Direct Materials - SF-001 $45,000

Cr. Direct Labor - SF-001 $32,000

Cr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $85,000

Cr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $4,200

Cr. Job Site Supervision - SF-001 $18,000

(Reclassify job costs to WIP asset)

WIP Liability Recognition

Project with billings exceeding earned revenue:

  • Progress Billings: $650,000
  • Costs Incurred: $480,000
  • Revenue Recognized: $600,000
  • WIP Liability: $650,000 - ($480,000 + $120,000) = $50,000

WIP Liability Entry:

Dr. Billings in Excess of Costs $50,000

Cr. Overbilled Revenue $50,000

(Recognize overbilled liability)

Month-End Accrual Entries

Unbilled Subcontractor Costs

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $25,000

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - MF-002 $18,500

Cr. Accrued Subcontractor Costs $43,500

(Accrue completed work not yet billed)

Equipment Usage Accruals

Dr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $3,400

Dr. Equipment Costs - MF-002 $5,100

Cr. Accrued Equipment Costs $8,500

(Accrue equipment usage for partial period)

Contract Completion Entries

Final Revenue Recognition

Dr. Accounts Receivable $94,750

Cr. Construction Revenue - SF-001 $94,750

(Final revenue to reach 100% completion)

WIP Clearance

Dr. Cost of Sales - SF-001 $680,000

Cr. Costs in Excess of Billings $680,000

(Clear WIP asset upon project completion)

Retainage Release

Dr. Cash $85,000

Cr. Accounts Receivable - Retainage $85,000

(Final retainage collection)

Week 3: Monthly and Year-End Closing Procedures

The Construction Closing Challenge

Construction closes are more complex than other industries due to:

  • Multiple projects at various completion stages
  • Complex WIP calculations requiring project manager input
  • Project-based cost allocation timing
  • Retainage and billing cycle variations
  • Multiple stakeholder reporting requirements

Monthly Closing Timeline

Pre-Close Activities (Ongoing)

Daily:

  • Post vendor invoices with proper job coding
  • Process timecards with project allocation
  • Update project progress in job costing system
  • Monitor cash receipts and customer applications
  • Reconcile credit card transactions to projects

Weekly:

  • Review WIP percentages with project managers
  • Process equipment usage reports and allocate costs
  • Update change order status and approvals
  • Review subcontractor progress and accrual needs
  • Analyze project cost trends and budget variances

Formal Monthly Close Process

Days 1-3: Data Collection and Validation

Day 1 Schedule:

8:00 AM - Project Manager Meeting

  • Review percentage complete estimates
  • Discuss approved but unprocessed change orders
  • Identify claims or disputes requiring accrual
  • Review cost-to-complete estimates and budget revisions

10:00 AM - Accounts Payable Review

  • Ensure all vendor invoices through month-end entered
  • Review receiving reports for uninvoiced deliveries
  • Verify job coding accuracy for significant purchases
  • Identify recurring expenses requiring accrual

2:00 PM - Payroll and Labor Cost Review

  • Finalize timecard approvals for month-end
  • Review labor allocation between projects and overhead
  • Calculate accrued vacation and benefit costs
  • Update certified payroll for prevailing wage projects

Day 2 Tasks:

Equipment and Overhead Allocation

  • Calculate equipment usage by project (hours/days)
  • Allocate overhead using predetermined allocation bases
  • Review insurance and utility costs for job site allocation
  • Process fuel and maintenance costs to equipment

Bank Reconciliation

  • Reconcile all bank accounts to general ledger
  • Identify and research outstanding items
  • Post bank fees or interest not previously recorded
  • Verify proper cutoff for deposits and checks

Week 4: Internal Controls and Documentation Requirements

Internal Control Framework for Construction

The COSO framework adapted for construction addresses unique risks in project-based operations.

Control Environment Components

1. Tone at the Top

  • Management integrity and ethical values
  • Commitment to competence and training
  • Board oversight and governance
  • Management philosophy and operating style

2. Risk Assessment Construction-specific risks requiring controls:

  • Cash disbursements (large, frequent payments)
  • Inventory management (multiple locations)
  • Equipment usage (valuable, mobile assets)
  • Payroll (high volume, multiple sites)
  • Change orders (dispute potential)
  • Revenue recognition (complex estimates)

Cash Disbursement Controls

Three-Way Match Procedure

Step-by-Step Process:

Step 1: Purchase Order Creation

  • Requisition approved by project manager
  • Purchase order created by purchasing department
  • PO includes vendor, description, quantity, price, delivery location, job code
  • Approval matrix enforced based on thresholds

Step 2: Receiving Process

  • Receiving department verifies delivery against PO
  • Receiving report documents date, quantity, condition, delivery location
  • Discrepancies reported immediately to purchasing
  • Receiving report forwarded to accounts payable

Step 3: Invoice Processing

  • AP matches: Purchase Order + Receiving Report + Vendor Invoice
  • Verifies quantities, prices, terms, mathematical accuracy
  • Codes invoice to proper GL account and job number
  • Routes to appropriate approver

Job Costing Controls

Time and Attendance Controls

Daily Process:

  1. Electronic time entry via mobile app/kiosks
  2. Supervisor validation and daily approval
  3. Project code verification for proper allocation
  4. Exception reporting for unusual patterns

Weekly Process:

  1. Project manager review of labor allocations
  2. Budget comparison (actual vs. budgeted hours)
  3. Productivity analysis (output per labor hour)
  4. Electronic approval before payroll processing

Material Control Procedures

Procurement Controls:

  • Maintain approved vendor list with annual reviews
  • Require competitive bidding for purchases >$5,000
  • Monitor vendor performance (delivery, quality, pricing)
  • Implement payment terms to optimize cash flow

Inventory Management:

  • Monthly cycle counts at each job site
  • Barcode scanning for material deliveries
  • Just-in-time delivery to reduce theft risk
  • Superintendent sign-off for material transfers

Revenue Recognition Controls

Percentage of Completion Verification

Monthly Process:

  1. Physical progress review with site visits and photos
  2. Cost analysis: actual vs. budgeted costs
  3. Estimate updates with project managers
  4. Independent review by controller
  5. Management approval by CFO

Information Technology Controls

System Access Controls:

  • User access rights based on job responsibilities
  • Quarterly review and update of permissions
  • Password requirements and regular changes
  • Activity logging for sensitive transactions

Data Backup and Recovery:

  • Daily automated backups of accounting system
  • Weekly verification of backup integrity
  • Quarterly disaster recovery testing
  • Cloud storage with encryption

Month 5 Quiz

Question 1: In a construction chart of accounts, the account "Costs in Excess of Billings" represents: a) Materials purchased but not used b) Work performed but not yet billed c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings d) Equipment costs allocated to projects

Answer: c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings

Explanation: This WIP asset account captures situations where total costs incurred plus gross profit recognized exceed the amount billed to customers, representing earned but unbilled revenue.

Question 2: Calculate the percentage complete and revenue recognition:

  • Contract Value: $1,200,000
  • Costs Incurred: $720,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $960,000
  • Progress Billings: $800,000

Answer:

  • Percentage Complete: $720,000 ÷ $960,000 = 75%
  • Revenue Earned: $1,200,000 × 75% = $900,000
  • WIP Position: ($720,000 + $180,000) - $800,000 = $100,000 asset

Question 3: Which segregation of duties violation creates the highest fraud risk? a) Same person prepares and signs checks b) Same person receives payments and makes deposits c) Same person approves POs and receives goods d) Same person enters timecards and calculates payroll

Answer: a) Same person prepares and signs checks

Explanation: This eliminates independent verification of payments and allows one person to initiate, approve, and execute transactions without oversight.

Question 4: Equipment depreciation in construction companies should be: a) Always recorded as operating expense b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction c) Recorded only when equipment is sold d) Never allocated to specific projects

Answer: b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction

Explanation: Construction equipment used on projects should have depreciation allocated as a direct cost to ensure proper job costing and project profitability analysis.

Question 5: The three-way match process includes: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice b) Budget, purchase order, payment c) Invoice, check, bank statement d) Timecard, payroll, tax deposit

Answer: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice

Explanation: Three-way matching verifies that goods ordered (PO) match goods received (receiving report) and goods invoiced (vendor invoice) before payment authorization.

Month 5 Case Study: Rocky Mountain Builders Chart of Accounts Implementation

Background

Rocky Mountain Builders, a $25M revenue construction company, is transitioning from QuickBooks to Ledgerline Intacct. As CFO, you must design and implement a comprehensive chart of accounts supporting growth to $75M over three years.

Company Profile

  • Revenue: $25M annually
  • Project Mix: 60% Single Family, 30% Multifamily, 10% Commercial
  • Geography: Colorado, Utah, Arizona
  • Employees: 85 (15 office, 70 field)
  • Active Projects: 15-20 concurrent
  • Structure: Parent LLC with project subsidiaries

Current Challenges

  • Inadequate job costing detail
  • Manual WIP calculations
  • Limited profitability tracking by project type
  • Poor integration between field and office
  • Difficulty with financial reporting

Implementation Requirements

Phase 1: Chart Design (Weeks 1-2) Design account numbering for:

  • Cost code integration (CSI format)

  • Equipment utilization tracking

Phase 2: System Setup (Weeks 3-4)

  • Configure Ledgerline Intacct multi-dimensional structure
  • Integrate with JCS Construction job costing
  • Setup automated workflows

Phase 3: Controls Implementation (Weeks 5-6)

  • Electronic purchase order system with approvals
  • Mobile timecard entry with GPS verification
  • Automated bank reconciliation
  • Exception-based reporting
  • Management dashboard creation

Expected Results

  • Reduce monthly close from 22 to 8 days
  • Improve WIP accuracy from ±15% to ±3%
  • Enable real-time project margin visibility
  • Automate 80% of routine accounting transactions
  • Provide executive dashboard for key metrics

Case Requirements

  1. Design complete chart of accounts with 100+ accounts
  2. Create implementation timeline with milestones
  3. Identify change management requirements
  4. Calculate ROI over 3-year period
  5. Develop training plan for 25 users
  6. Design control testing procedures

Month 6: Financial Close - Month-End and Quarter-End Procedures

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 6, you will:

  • Master advanced month-end close optimization techniques
  • Implement real-time WIP schedule optimization and project tracking
  • Execute comprehensive quarter-end procedures and compliance reporting
  • Integrate technology and automation for closing excellence
  • Achieve industry-leading close cycle times while maintaining accuracy

Overview

Financial closes in construction are more complex than other industries due to project-based operations, work-in-progress calculations, and multiple stakeholder reporting needs. This month transforms your closing process from a time-consuming manual effort to a streamlined, automated system that provides timely, accurate financial information for strategic decision-making.

Construction CFO Training Curriculum - Months 5-8

Comprehensive Textbook Manuscript

Month 5: General Ledger, Chart of Accounts, and Journal Entries

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 5, you will:

  • Design comprehensive chart of accounts tailored for construction operations
  • Master the integration between general ledger accounts and job costing systems
  • Execute standard journal entries for construction operations with precision
  • Implement advanced month-end closing procedures and controls
  • Establish robust internal controls and documentation requirements

Overview

The general ledger serves as the foundation of construction accounting, but unlike other industries, construction requires specialized account structures that accommodate project-based operations, work-in-progress tracking, and complex cost allocation. This month builds your expertise in designing, implementing, and managing sophisticated general ledger systems that support both financial reporting and operational decision-making.

Week 1: Construction-Specific Chart of Accounts Design

The Strategic Foundation of Construction Accounting

The chart of accounts is not merely a list of accounts—it's the architectural blueprint of your financial system. In construction, this blueprint must accommodate unique industry characteristics while maintaining the flexibility to scale with business growth.

Core Principles of Construction Chart of Accounts

1. Project Integration Every account must seamlessly integrate with job costing systems. Consider this example:

Account 5100 - Direct Labor

  • Must track labor by project
  • Should accommodate phase/cost code breakdowns
  • Must integrate with payroll systems
  • Should support equipment hour allocation

2. Multi-Dimensional Flexibility Modern construction accounting requires multi-dimensional tracking:

Dimension Examples:

  • Entity: Multiple legal entities or divisions
  • Project: Individual jobs or contracts
  • Cost Code: CSI-based cost categorization
  • Phase: Construction sequence tracking
  • Location: Geographic or site-specific

Comprehensive Account Structure Framework

ASSETS (1000-1999)

Current Assets (1000-1499)

Cash and Cash Equivalents (1000-1099)

1000 - Operating Cash - Primary checking account

1010 - Payroll Cash - Dedicated payroll account

1020 - Project Cash - Customer deposits and escrows

1025 - Retainage Cash - Restricted cash for retainage

1030 - Money Market - Short-term liquid investments

1040 - Petty Cash - Job site cash funds

1050 - Restricted Cash - Letter of credit deposits

Why This Structure Matters: Segregating cash by purpose provides better cash flow management and reduces reconciliation complexity. The CFO needs immediate visibility into available operating cash versus restricted funds.

Accounts Receivable (1100-1199)

1100 - Accounts Receivable - Trade (current billings)

1110 - Accounts Receivable - Retainage (5-10% withheld)

1115 - Accounts Receivable - Long-term Retainage (due >1 year)

1120 - Unbilled Receivables - Earned but not billed

1125 - Notes Receivable - Customer financing arrangements

1130 - Employee Advances - Travel and expense advances

1140 - Other Receivables - Claims, insurance, etc.

1150 - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts - Contra asset

Critical CFO Insight: Retainage timing drives cash flow. Separate current (due within 1 year) from long-term retainage for accurate liquidity analysis.

Work-in-Progress and Inventory (1200-1399)

1200 - Raw Materials Inventory - Lumber, steel, concrete

1210 - Supplies Inventory - Small tools, safety equipment

1220 - Work in Process - Job cost accumulation

1250 - Costs in Excess of Billings - WIP asset (overbilled work)

1260 - Contract Assets - ASC 606 contract assets

1300 - Land Held for Development - Future projects

1310 - Construction in Progress - Assets for own use

The WIP Connection: Account 1250 is crucial for revenue recognition. When costs incurred plus recognized profit exceed customer billings, this account captures the asset representing work performed but not yet billed.

LIABILITIES (2000-2999)

Current Liabilities (2000-2499)

Trade Payables (2000-2099)

2000 - Accounts Payable - Trade vendors

2010 - Accounts Payable - Subcontractors

2020 - Retainage Payable - Amounts withheld from subs

2025 - Contract Retainage Payable - Customer retainage held

2030 - Accrued Trade Payables - Goods received, not invoiced

Customer-Related Liabilities (2200-2299)

2200 - Billings in Excess of Costs - WIP liability (underbilled work)

2210 - Customer Deposits - Advance payments received

2215 - Contract Liabilities - ASC 606 contract liabilities

2220 - Warranty Reserve - Future warranty obligations

2230 - Contract Completion Reserve - Punch list items

REVENUE (4000-4999)

Construction Revenue by Type (4000-4499)

4000 - Single-Family Construction Revenue

4100 - Multifamily Construction Revenue

4200 - Commercial Construction Revenue

4300 - Renovation/Remodel Revenue

4400 - Change Order Revenue - Contract modifications

4450 - Claims Revenue - Disputed/extra work

4500 - Service Revenue - Maintenance, warranty

Revenue Recognition Note: Under ASC 606, all construction revenue should use percentage-of-completion method. Separate revenue types enable margin analysis and project profitability tracking.

COST OF SALES (5000-5999)

Direct Construction Costs by Type (5000-5399)

5000 - Direct Materials - Single Family

5010 - Direct Materials - Multifamily

5020 - Direct Materials - Commercial

5100 - Direct Labor - Single Family

5110 - Direct Labor - Multifamily

5120 - Direct Labor - Commercial

5200 - Subcontractors - Single Family

5210 - Subcontractors - Multifamily

5220 - Subcontractors - Commercial

5300 - Equipment Costs - Allocated to jobs

5310 - Fuel and Maintenance - Job-specific

5320 - Permits and Fees - Project-specific

Job Costing Integration Framework

The chart of accounts must integrate with job costing through dimensional coding:

Example Project Coding:

Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Project: SF-2024-001 (Single Family project)

Cost Code: 06110 (Rough Carpentry)

Phase: 03 (Framing)

Full Code: 5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

WIP Account Relationships

Critical Formula:

WIP Asset = (Costs Incurred + Gross Profit Recognized) - Progress Billings

When positive: Use Account 1250 (Costs in Excess of Billings) When negative: Use Account 2200 (Billings in Excess of Costs)

Technology Integration

Modern systems like Ledgerline Intacct support dimensional accounting:

Example Configuration:

Base Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Entity Dimension: CS (Construction Services)

Project Dimension: SF-2024-001

Cost Code Dimension: 06110

Phase Dimension: 03

Result: CS-5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

Week 2: Standard Journal Entries for Construction Operations

Master Framework for Construction Journal Entries

Construction accounting requires specialized journal entries that capture the unique nature of project-based operations, long-term contracts, and complex cost allocations.

Revenue Recognition Entries

Percentage-of-Completion Revenue Recognition

Scenario: Mountain View Homes Project

  • Contract Amount: $850,000
  • Costs Incurred to Date: $425,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $680,000
  • Previously Recognized Revenue: $250,000

Step 1: Calculate Percentage Complete

Percentage Complete = $425,000 ÷ $680,000 = 62.5%

Step 2: Calculate Total Revenue Earned

Total Revenue Earned = $850,000 × 62.5% = $531,250

Step 3: Calculate Current Period Revenue

Current Period Revenue = $531,250 - $250,000 = $281,250

Journal Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable $281,250

Cr. Construction Revenue - SF $281,250

(To recognize revenue based on percentage completion)

Progress Billing Entries

Scenario: Monthly progress billing with retainage

  • Work completed: $281,250
  • Customer retainage: 10%
  • Previous unpaid billings: $125,000

Progress Billing Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable - Trade $253,125

Dr. Accounts Receivable - Retainage $28,125

Cr. Billings on Construction Contracts $281,250

(Progress billing with 10% retainage withheld)

Collection Entry:

Dr. Cash $378,125

Cr. Accounts Receivable - Trade $378,125

(Collection of current and previous billings)

Change Order Revenue Recognition

Scenario: Customer-approved change order

  • Original contract: $850,000
  • Approved change order: $75,000
  • Change order work 60% complete

Change Order Revenue Entry:

Dr. Contract Asset - Change Orders $45,000

Cr. Change Order Revenue $45,000

(60% completion of $75,000 change order)

Cost Recording and Allocation Entries

Material Purchase and Allocation

Initial Purchase:

Dr. Raw Materials Inventory $125,000

Cr. Accounts Payable - Trade $125,000

(Lumber and concrete purchases)

Material Requisition to Projects:

Dr. Direct Materials - SF-001 $45,000

Dr. Direct Materials - MF-002 $55,000

Dr. Direct Materials - CC-003 $25,000

Cr. Raw Materials Inventory $125,000

(Allocate materials to specific projects)

Direct Labor Allocation

Comprehensive Payroll Entry

Weekly payroll processing:

Dr. Direct Labor - SF-001 $32,000

Dr. Direct Labor - MF-002 $48,000

Dr. Job Site Supervision $18,000

Dr. Administrative Salaries $12,000

Cr. Wages Payable $82,500

Cr. Federal Tax Withholding $16,500

Cr. State Tax Withholding $4,125

Cr. FICA Payable $6,875

Cr. Medicare Payable $1,608

Cr. 401k Employee Deferrals $2,750

Cr. Health Insurance Employee Share $4,640

(Payroll distribution across projects and overhead)

Payroll Tax Burden:

Dr. Direct Labor - SF-001 (Burden) $3,200

Dr. Direct Labor - MF-002 (Burden) $4,800

Dr. Job Site Supervision (Burden) $1,800

Dr. Payroll Tax Expense (Admin) $1,200

Cr. FICA Payable - Employer $6,875

Cr. Medicare Payable - Employer $1,608

Cr. FUTA Payable $660

Cr. SUTA Payable $1,857

(Employer payroll taxes by project and overhead)

Subcontractor Cost Recognition

Approved subcontractor invoice with retainage:

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $85,000

Cr. Accounts Payable - Subcontractors $76,500

Cr. Retainage Payable $8,500

(Plumbing subcontractor with 10% retainage)

Equipment Cost Allocation

Monthly Equipment Usage Allocation

Equipment depreciation and usage tracking:

Dr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $4,200

Dr. Equipment Costs - MF-002 $6,800

Dr. Equipment Costs - CC-003 $2,500

Dr. Equipment Depreciation - Office $1,500

Cr. Accumulated Depreciation - Equipment $15,000

(Allocate equipment depreciation based on usage)

Work-in-Progress Entries

WIP Asset Recognition

Project with costs exceeding billings:

  • Costs Incurred: $425,000
  • Revenue Recognized: $531,250
  • Progress Billings: $475,000
  • Gross Profit: $106,250
  • WIP Asset: ($425,000 + $106,250) - $475,000 = $56,250

WIP Asset Entry:

Dr. Costs in Excess of Billings $56,250

Cr. Direct Materials - SF-001 $45,000

Cr. Direct Labor - SF-001 $32,000

Cr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $85,000

Cr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $4,200

Cr. Job Site Supervision - SF-001 $18,000

(Reclassify job costs to WIP asset)

WIP Liability Recognition

Project with billings exceeding earned revenue:

  • Progress Billings: $650,000
  • Costs Incurred: $480,000
  • Revenue Recognized: $600,000
  • WIP Liability: $650,000 - ($480,000 + $120,000) = $50,000

WIP Liability Entry:

Dr. Billings in Excess of Costs $50,000

Cr. Overbilled Revenue $50,000

(Recognize overbilled liability)

Month-End Accrual Entries

Unbilled Subcontractor Costs

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - SF-001 $25,000

Dr. Subcontractor Costs - MF-002 $18,500

Cr. Accrued Subcontractor Costs $43,500

(Accrue completed work not yet billed)

Equipment Usage Accruals

Dr. Equipment Costs - SF-001 $3,400

Dr. Equipment Costs - MF-002 $5,100

Cr. Accrued Equipment Costs $8,500

(Accrue equipment usage for partial period)

Contract Completion Entries

Final Revenue Recognition

Dr. Accounts Receivable $94,750

Cr. Construction Revenue - SF-001 $94,750

(Final revenue to reach 100% completion)

WIP Clearance

Dr. Cost of Sales - SF-001 $680,000

Cr. Costs in Excess of Billings $680,000

(Clear WIP asset upon project completion)

Retainage Release

Dr. Cash $85,000

Cr. Accounts Receivable - Retainage $85,000

(Final retainage collection)

Week 3: Monthly and Year-End Closing Procedures

The Construction Closing Challenge

Construction closes are more complex than other industries due to:

  • Multiple projects at various completion stages
  • Complex WIP calculations requiring project manager input
  • Project-based cost allocation timing
  • Retainage and billing cycle variations
  • Multiple stakeholder reporting requirements

Monthly Closing Timeline

Pre-Close Activities (Ongoing)

Daily:

  • Post vendor invoices with proper job coding
  • Process timecards with project allocation
  • Update project progress in job costing system
  • Monitor cash receipts and customer applications
  • Reconcile credit card transactions to projects

Weekly:

  • Review WIP percentages with project managers
  • Process equipment usage reports and allocate costs
  • Update change order status and approvals
  • Review subcontractor progress and accrual needs

Month 5 Quiz

Question 1: In a construction chart of accounts, the account "Costs in Excess of Billings" represents: a) Materials purchased but not used b) Work performed but not yet billed c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings d) Equipment costs allocated to projects

Answer: c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings

Explanation: This WIP asset account captures situations where total costs incurred plus gross profit recognized exceed the amount billed to customers, representing earned but unbilled revenue.

Question 2: Calculate the percentage complete and revenue recognition:

  • Contract Value: $1,200,000
  • Costs Incurred: $720,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $960,000
  • Progress Billings: $800,000

Answer:

  • Percentage Complete: $720,000 ÷ $960,000 = 75%
  • Revenue Earned: $1,200,000 × 75% = $900,000
  • WIP Position: ($720,000 + $180,000) - $800,000 = $100,000 asset

Question 3: Which segregation of duties violation creates the highest fraud risk? a) Same person prepares and signs checks b) Same person receives payments and makes deposits c) Same person approves POs and receives goods d) Same person enters timecards and calculates payroll

Answer: a) Same person prepares and signs checks

Explanation: This eliminates independent verification of payments and allows one person to initiate, approve, and execute transactions without oversight.

Question 4: Equipment depreciation in construction companies should be: a) Always recorded as operating expense b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction c) Recorded only when equipment is sold d) Never allocated to specific projects

Answer: b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction

Explanation: Construction equipment used on projects should have depreciation allocated as a direct cost to ensure proper job costing and project profitability analysis.

Question 5: The three-way match process includes: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice b) Budget, purchase order, payment c) Invoice, check, bank statement d) Timecard, payroll, tax deposit

Answer: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice

Explanation: Three-way matching verifies that goods ordered (PO) match goods received (receiving report) and goods invoiced (vendor invoice) before payment authorization.

1. Design a chart of accounts structure for a construction company with single-family, multifamily, and commercial divisions. Include at least 15 accounts with proper numbering and explain the rationale for your structure.

  • Direct labor incurred: $85,000

  • Project B: Costs $300k, Contract $500k, 50% complete, Billings $280k
  • Project C: Costs $200k, Contract $350k, 40% complete, Billings $160k

5. Explain the difference between "Costs in Excess of Billings" and "Billings in Excess of Costs" and when each account is used.

Month 5 Case Study: Rocky Mountain Builders Chart of Accounts Implementation

Background

Rocky Mountain Builders, a $25M revenue construction company, is transitioning from QuickBooks to Ledgerline Intacct. As CFO, you must design and implement a comprehensive chart of accounts supporting growth to $75M over three years.

Company Profile

  • Revenue: $25M annually
  • Project Mix: 60% Single Family, 30% Multifamily, 10% Commercial
  • Geography: Colorado, Utah, Arizona
  • Employees: 85 (15 office, 70 field)
  • Active Projects: 15-20 concurrent
  • Structure: Parent LLC with project subsidiaries

Current Challenges

  • Inadequate job costing detail
  • Manual WIP calculations
  • Limited profitability tracking by project type
  • Poor integration between field and office
  • Difficulty with financial reporting

Implementation Requirements

Phase 1: Chart Design (Weeks 1-2) Design account numbering for:

  • Multi-entity structure (holding company + operating entities)
  • Project-specific tracking
  • Cost code integration (CSI format)
  • Phase-based reporting
  • Equipment utilization tracking

Phase 2: System Setup (Weeks 3-4)

  • Configure Ledgerline Intacct multi-dimensional structure
  • Integrate with JCS Construction job costing
  • Setup automated workflows
  • Design custom reporting
  • Migrate 2 years historical data

Phase 3: Controls Implementation (Weeks 5-6)

  • Electronic purchase order system with approvals
  • Mobile timecard entry with GPS verification
  • Automated bank reconciliation
  • Exception-based reporting
  • Management dashboard creation

Expected Results

  • Reduce monthly close from 22 to 8 days
  • Improve WIP accuracy from ±15% to ±3%
  • Enable real-time project margin visibility
  • Automate 80% of routine accounting transactions
  • Provide executive dashboard for key metrics

Case Requirements

  1. Design complete chart of accounts with 100+ accounts
  2. Create implementation timeline with milestones
  3. Identify change management requirements
  4. Calculate ROI over 3-year period
  5. Develop training plan for 25 users
  6. Design control testing procedures

Month 6: Financial Close - Month-End and Quarter-End Procedures

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 6, you will:

  • Master advanced month-end close optimization techniques
  • Implement real-time WIP schedule optimization and project tracking
  • Execute comprehensive quarter-end procedures and compliance reporting
  • Integrate technology and automation for closing excellence
  • Achieve industry-leading close cycle times while maintaining accuracy

Overview

Financial closes in construction are more complex than other industries due to project-based operations, work-in-progress calculations, and multiple stakeholder reporting needs. This month transforms your closing process from a time-consuming manual effort to a streamlined, automated system that provides timely, accurate financial information for strategic decision-making.

Construction CFO Training Curriculum - Months 5-8

Comprehensive Textbook Manuscript

Month 5: General Ledger, Chart of Accounts, and Journal Entries

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 5, you will:

  • Design comprehensive chart of accounts tailored for construction operations
  • Master the integration between general ledger accounts and job costing systems
  • Execute standard journal entries for construction operations with precision
  • Implement advanced month-end closing procedures and controls
  • Establish robust internal controls and documentation requirements

Overview

The general ledger serves as the foundation of construction accounting, but unlike other industries, construction requires specialized account structures that accommodate project-based operations, work-in-progress tracking, and complex cost allocation. This month builds your expertise in designing, implementing, and managing sophisticated general ledger systems that support both financial reporting and operational decision-making.

Week 1: Construction-Specific Chart of Accounts Design

The Strategic Foundation of Construction Accounting

The chart of accounts is not merely a list of accounts—it's the architectural blueprint of your financial system. In construction, this blueprint must accommodate unique industry characteristics while maintaining the flexibility to scale with business growth.

Core Principles of Construction Chart of Accounts

1. Project Integration Every account must seamlessly integrate with job costing systems. Consider this example:

Account 5100 - Direct Labor

  • Must track labor by project
  • Should accommodate phase/cost code breakdowns
  • Must integrate with payroll systems
  • Should support equipment hour allocation

2. Multi-Dimensional Flexibility Modern construction accounting requires multi-dimensional tracking:

Dimension Examples:

  • Entity: Multiple legal entities or divisions
  • Project: Individual jobs or contracts
  • Cost Code: CSI-based cost categorization
  • Phase: Construction sequence tracking
  • Location: Geographic or site-specific

Comprehensive Account Structure Framework

ASSETS (1000-1999)

Current Assets (1000-1499)

Cash and Cash Equivalents (1000-1099)

1000 - Operating Cash - Primary checking account

1010 - Payroll Cash - Dedicated payroll account

1020 - Project Cash - Customer deposits and escrows

1025 - Retainage Cash - Restricted cash for retainage

1030 - Money Market - Short-term liquid investments

1040 - Petty Cash - Job site cash funds

1050 - Restricted Cash - Letter of credit deposits

Why This Structure Matters: Segregating cash by purpose provides better cash flow management and reduces reconciliation complexity. The CFO needs immediate visibility into available operating cash versus restricted funds.

Accounts Receivable (1100-1199)

1100 - Accounts Receivable - Trade (current billings)

1110 - Accounts Receivable - Retainage (5-10% withheld)

1115 - Accounts Receivable - Long-term Retainage (due >1 year)

1120 - Unbilled Receivables - Earned but not billed

1125 - Notes Receivable - Customer financing arrangements

1130 - Employee Advances - Travel and expense advances

1140 - Other Receivables - Claims, insurance, etc.

1150 - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts - Contra asset

Critical CFO Insight: Retainage timing drives cash flow. Separate current (due within 1 year) from long-term retainage for accurate liquidity analysis.

Work-in-Progress and Inventory (1200-1399)

1200 - Raw Materials Inventory - Lumber, steel, concrete

1210 - Supplies Inventory - Small tools, safety equipment

1220 - Work in Process - Job cost accumulation

1250 - Costs in Excess of Billings - WIP asset (overbilled work)

1260 - Contract Assets - ASC 606 contract assets

1300 - Land Held for Development - Future projects

1310 - Construction in Progress - Assets for own use

The WIP Connection: Account 1250 is crucial for revenue recognition. When costs incurred plus recognized profit exceed customer billings, this account captures the asset representing work performed but not yet billed.

LIABILITIES (2000-2999)

Current Liabilities (2000-2499)

Trade Payables (2000-2099)

2000 - Accounts Payable - Trade vendors

2010 - Accounts Payable - Subcontractors

2020 - Retainage Payable - Amounts withheld from subs

2025 - Contract Retainage Payable - Customer retainage held

2030 - Accrued Trade Payables - Goods received, not invoiced

Customer-Related Liabilities (2200-2299)

2200 - Billings in Excess of Costs - WIP liability (underbilled work)

2210 - Customer Deposits - Advance payments received

2215 - Contract Liabilities - ASC 606 contract liabilities

2220 - Warranty Reserve - Future warranty obligations

2230 - Contract Completion Reserve - Punch list items

REVENUE (4000-4999)

Construction Revenue by Type (4000-4499)

4000 - Single-Family Construction Revenue

4100 - Multifamily Construction Revenue

4200 - Commercial Construction Revenue

4300 - Renovation/Remodel Revenue

4400 - Change Order Revenue - Contract modifications

Month 5 Quiz

Question 1: In a construction chart of accounts, the account "Costs in Excess of Billings" represents: a) Materials purchased but not used b) Work performed but not yet billed c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings d) Equipment costs allocated to projects

Answer: c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings

Explanation: This WIP asset account captures situations where total costs incurred plus gross profit recognized exceed the amount billed to customers, representing earned but unbilled revenue.

Question 2: Calculate the percentage complete and revenue recognition:

  • Contract Value: $1,200,000
  • Costs Incurred: $720,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $960,000
  • Progress Billings: $800,000

Answer:

  • Percentage Complete: $720,000 ÷ $960,000 = 75%
  • Revenue Earned: $1,200,000 × 75% = $900,000
  • WIP Position: ($720,000 + $180,000) - $800,000 = $100,000 asset

Question 3: Which segregation of duties violation creates the highest fraud risk? a) Same person prepares and signs checks b) Same person receives payments and makes deposits c) Same person approves POs and receives goods d) Same person enters timecards and calculates payroll

Answer: a) Same person prepares and signs checks

Explanation: This eliminates independent verification of payments and allows one person to initiate, approve, and execute transactions without oversight.

Question 4: Equipment depreciation in construction companies should be: a) Always recorded as operating expense b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction c) Recorded only when equipment is sold d) Never allocated to specific projects

Answer: b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction

Explanation: Construction equipment used on projects should have depreciation allocated as a direct cost to ensure proper job costing and project profitability analysis.

Question 5: The three-way match process includes: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice b) Budget, purchase order, payment c) Invoice, check, bank statement d) Timecard, payroll, tax deposit

Answer: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice

Explanation: Three-way matching verifies that goods ordered (PO) match goods received (receiving report) and goods invoiced (vendor invoice) before payment authorization.

Month 5 Case Study: Rocky Mountain Builders Chart of Accounts Implementation

Background

Rocky Mountain Builders, a $25M revenue construction company, is transitioning from QuickBooks to Ledgerline Intacct. As CFO, you must design and implement a comprehensive chart of accounts supporting growth to $75M over three years.

Company Profile

  • Revenue: $25M annually
  • Project Mix: 60% Single Family, 30% Multifamily, 10% Commercial
  • Geography: Colorado, Utah, Arizona
  • Employees: 85 (15 office, 70 field)
  • Active Projects: 15-20 concurrent
  • Structure: Parent LLC with project subsidiaries

Current Challenges

  • Inadequate job costing detail
  • Manual WIP calculations
  • Limited profitability tracking by project type
  • Poor integration between field and office
  • Difficulty with financial reporting

Implementation Requirements

Phase 1: Chart Design (Weeks 1-2) Design account numbering for:

  • Multi-entity structure (holding company + operating entities)
  • Project-specific tracking
  • Cost code integration (CSI format)
  • Phase-based reporting
  • Equipment utilization tracking

Phase 2: System Setup (Weeks 3-4)

  • Configure Ledgerline Intacct multi-dimensional structure
  • Integrate with JCS Construction job costing
  • Setup automated workflows
  • Design custom reporting
  • Migrate 2 years historical data

Phase 3: Controls Implementation (Weeks 5-6)

  • Electronic purchase order system with approvals
  • Mobile timecard entry with GPS verification
  • Automated bank reconciliation
  • Exception-based reporting
  • Management dashboard creation

Expected Results

  • Reduce monthly close from 22 to 8 days
  • Improve WIP accuracy from ±15% to ±3%
  • Enable real-time project margin visibility
  • Automate 80% of routine accounting transactions
  • Provide executive dashboard for key metrics

Case Requirements

  1. Design complete chart of accounts with 100+ accounts
  2. Create implementation timeline with milestones
  3. Identify change management requirements
  4. Calculate ROI over 3-year period
  5. Develop training plan for 25 users
  6. Design control testing procedures

Month 6: Financial Close - Month-End and Quarter-End Procedures

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 6, you will:

  • Master advanced month-end close optimization techniques
  • Implement real-time WIP schedule optimization and project tracking
  • Execute comprehensive quarter-end procedures and compliance reporting
  • Integrate technology and automation for closing excellence
  • Achieve industry-leading close cycle times while maintaining accuracy

Overview

Financial closes in construction are more complex than other industries due to project-based operations, work-in-progress calculations, and multiple stakeholder reporting needs. This month transforms your closing process from a time-consuming manual effort to a streamlined, automated system that provides timely, accurate financial information for strategic decision-making.

Construction CFO Training Curriculum - Months 5-8

Comprehensive Textbook Manuscript

Month 5: General Ledger, Chart of Accounts, and Journal Entries

Learning Objectives

By the end of Month 5, you will:

  • Design comprehensive chart of accounts tailored for construction operations
  • Master the integration between general ledger accounts and job costing systems
  • Execute standard journal entries for construction operations with precision
  • Implement advanced month-end closing procedures and controls
  • Establish robust internal controls and documentation requirements

Overview

The general ledger serves as the foundation of construction accounting, but unlike other industries, construction requires specialized account structures that accommodate project-based operations, work-in-progress tracking, and complex cost allocation. This month builds your expertise in designing, implementing, and managing sophisticated general ledger systems that support both financial reporting and operational decision-making.

Week 1: Construction-Specific Chart of Accounts Design

The Strategic Foundation of Construction Accounting

The chart of accounts is not merely a list of accounts—it's the architectural blueprint of your financial system. In construction, this blueprint must accommodate unique industry characteristics while maintaining the flexibility to scale with business growth.

Core Principles of Construction Chart of Accounts

1. Project Integration Every account must seamlessly integrate with job costing systems. Consider this example:

Account 5100 - Direct Labor

  • Must track labor by project
  • Should accommodate phase/cost code breakdowns
  • Must integrate with payroll systems
  • Should support equipment hour allocation

2. Multi-Dimensional Flexibility Modern construction accounting requires multi-dimensional tracking:

Dimension Examples:

  • Entity: Multiple legal entities or divisions
  • Project: Individual jobs or contracts
  • Cost Code: CSI-based cost categorization
  • Phase: Construction sequence tracking
  • Location: Geographic or site-specific

Comprehensive Account Structure Framework

ASSETS (1000-1999)

Current Assets (1000-1499)

Cash and Cash Equivalents (1000-1099)

1000 - Operating Cash - Primary checking account

1010 - Payroll Cash - Dedicated payroll account

1020 - Project Cash - Customer deposits and escrows

1025 - Retainage Cash - Restricted cash for retainage

1030 - Money Market - Short-term liquid investments

1040 - Petty Cash - Job site cash funds

1050 - Restricted Cash - Letter of credit deposits

Why This Structure Matters: Segregating cash by purpose provides better cash flow management and reduces reconciliation complexity. The CFO needs immediate visibility into available operating cash versus restricted funds.

Accounts Receivable (1100-1199)

1100 - Accounts Receivable - Trade (current billings)

1110 - Accounts Receivable - Retainage (5-10% withheld)

1115 - Accounts Receivable - Long-term Retainage (due >1 year)

1120 - Unbilled Receivables - Earned but not billed

1125 - Notes Receivable - Customer financing arrangements

1130 - Employee Advances - Travel and expense advances

1140 - Other Receivables - Claims, insurance, etc.

1150 - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts - Contra asset

Critical CFO Insight: Retainage timing drives cash flow. Separate current (due within 1 year) from long-term retainage for accurate liquidity analysis.

Work-in-Progress and Inventory (1200-1399)

1200 - Raw Materials Inventory - Lumber, steel, concrete

1210 - Supplies Inventory - Small tools, safety equipment

1220 - Work in Process - Job cost accumulation

1250 - Costs in Excess of Billings - WIP asset (overbilled work)

1260 - Contract Assets - ASC 606 contract assets

1300 - Land Held for Development - Future projects

1310 - Construction in Progress - Assets for own use

The WIP Connection: Account 1250 is crucial for revenue recognition. When costs incurred plus recognized profit exceed customer billings, this account captures the asset representing work performed but not yet billed.

LIABILITIES (2000-2999)

Current Liabilities (2000-2499)

Trade Payables (2000-2099)

2000 - Accounts Payable - Trade vendors

2010 - Accounts Payable - Subcontractors

2020 - Retainage Payable - Amounts withheld from subs

2025 - Contract Retainage Payable - Customer retainage held

2030 - Accrued Trade Payables - Goods received, not invoiced

Customer-Related Liabilities (2200-2299)

2200 - Billings in Excess of Costs - WIP liability (underbilled work)

2210 - Customer Deposits - Advance payments received

2215 - Contract Liabilities - ASC 606 contract liabilities

2220 - Warranty Reserve - Future warranty obligations

2230 - Contract Completion Reserve - Punch list items

REVENUE (4000-4999)

Construction Revenue by Type (4000-4499)

4000 - Single-Family Construction Revenue

4100 - Multifamily Construction Revenue

4200 - Commercial Construction Revenue

4300 - Renovation/Remodel Revenue

4400 - Change Order Revenue - Contract modifications

4450 - Claims Revenue - Disputed/extra work

4500 - Service Revenue - Maintenance, warranty

Revenue Recognition Note: Under ASC 606, all construction revenue should use percentage-of-completion method. Separate revenue types enable margin analysis and project profitability tracking.

COST OF SALES (5000-5999)

Direct Construction Costs by Type (5000-5399)

5000 - Direct Materials - Single Family

5010 - Direct Materials - Multifamily

5020 - Direct Materials - Commercial

5100 - Direct Labor - Single Family

5110 - Direct Labor - Multifamily

5120 - Direct Labor - Commercial

5200 - Subcontractors - Single Family

5210 - Subcontractors - Multifamily

5220 - Subcontractors - Commercial

5300 - Equipment Costs - Allocated to jobs

5310 - Fuel and Maintenance - Job-specific

5320 - Permits and Fees - Project-specific

Job Costing Integration Framework

The chart of accounts must integrate with job costing through dimensional coding:

Example Project Coding:

Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Project: SF-2024-001 (Single Family project)

Cost Code: 06110 (Rough Carpentry)

Phase: 03 (Framing)

Full Code: 5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

WIP Account Relationships

Critical Formula:

WIP Asset = (Costs Incurred + Gross Profit Recognized) - Progress Billings

When positive: Use Account 1250 (Costs in Excess of Billings) When negative: Use Account 2200 (Billings in Excess of Costs)

Technology Integration

Modern systems like Ledgerline Intacct support dimensional accounting:

Example Configuration:

Base Account: 5100 (Direct Labor)

Entity Dimension: CS (Construction Services)

Project Dimension: SF-2024-001

Cost Code Dimension: 06110

Phase Dimension: 03

Result: CS-5100-SF-2024-001-06110-03

Week 2: Standard Journal Entries for Construction Operations

Master Framework for Construction Journal Entries

Construction accounting requires specialized journal entries that capture the unique nature of project-based operations, long-term contracts, and complex cost allocations.

Revenue Recognition Entries

Percentage-of-Completion Revenue Recognition

Scenario: Mountain View Homes Project

  • Contract Amount: $850,000
  • Costs Incurred to Date: $425,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $680,000
  • Previously Recognized Revenue: $250,000

Step 1: Calculate Percentage Complete

Percentage Complete = $425,000 ÷ $680,000 = 62.5%

Step 2: Calculate Total Revenue Earned

Total Revenue Earned = $850,000 × 62.5% = $531,250

Step 3: Calculate Current Period Revenue

Current Period Revenue = $531,250 - $250,000 = $281,250

Journal Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable $281,250

Cr. Construction Revenue - SF $281,250

(To recognize revenue based on percentage completion)

Progress Billing Entries

Scenario: Monthly progress billing with retainage

  • Work completed: $281,250
  • Customer retainage: 10%
  • Previous unpaid billings: $125,000

Progress Billing Entry:

Dr. Accounts Receivable - Trade $253,125

Collection Entry:

Change Order Revenue Recognition

Work-in-Progress Entries

WIP Asset Recognition

Project with costs exceeding billings:

  • Costs Incurred: $425,000
  • Revenue Recognized: $531,250
  • Progress Billings: $475,000
  • Gross Profit: $106,250
  • WIP Asset: ($425,000 + $106,250) - $475,000 = $56,250

  • WIP Liability: $650,000 - ($480,000 + $120,000) = $50,000

WIP Liability Entry:

Month-End Accrual Entries

Final Revenue Recognition

Week 3: Monthly and Year-End Closing Procedures

The Construction Closing Challenge

Construction closes are more complex than other industries due to:

  • Multiple projects at various completion stages
  • Complex WIP calculations requiring project manager input
  • Project-based cost allocation timing
  • Retainage and billing cycle variations
  • Multiple stakeholder reporting requirements

Monthly Closing Timeline

Pre-Close Activities (Ongoing)

Daily:

  • Post vendor invoices with proper job coding
  • Process timecards with project allocation
  • Update project progress in job costing system
  • Monitor cash receipts and customer applications
  • Reconcile credit card transactions to projects

Weekly:

  • Review WIP percentages with project managers
  • Process equipment usage reports and allocate costs
  • Update change order status and approvals
  • Review subcontractor progress and accrual needs
  • Analyze project cost trends and budget variances

Formal Monthly Close Process

  • Discuss approved but unprocessed change orders

  • Ensure all vendor invoices through month-end entered
  • Review receiving reports for uninvoiced deliveries
  • Verify job coding accuracy for significant purchases
  • Identify recurring expenses requiring accrual

  • Finalize timecard approvals for month-end
  • Review labor allocation between projects and overhead
  • Calculate accrued vacation and benefit costs
  • Update certified payroll for prevailing wage projects

Day 2 Tasks:

  • Calculate equipment usage by project (hours/days)
  • Allocate overhead using predetermined allocation bases
  • Review insurance and utility costs for job site allocation
  • Process fuel and maintenance costs to equipment

Bank Reconciliation

  • Reconcile all bank accounts to general ledger
  • Identify and research outstanding items
  • Post bank fees or interest not previously recorded
  • Verify proper cutoff for deposits and checks

Week 4: Internal Controls and Documentation Requirements

Internal Control Framework for Construction

The COSO framework adapted for construction addresses unique risks in project-based operations.

Control Environment Components

1. Tone at the Top

  • Management integrity and ethical values
  • Commitment to competence and training
  • Board oversight and governance
  • Management philosophy and operating style

2. Risk Assessment Construction-specific risks requiring controls:

  • Cash disbursements (large, frequent payments)
  • Inventory management (multiple locations)
  • Equipment usage (valuable, mobile assets)
  • Payroll (high volume, multiple sites)
  • Change orders (dispute potential)
  • Revenue recognition (complex estimates)

Cash Disbursement Controls

Three-Way Match Procedure

Step-by-Step Process:

Step 1: Purchase Order Creation

  • Requisition approved by project manager
  • Purchase order created by purchasing department
  • PO includes vendor, description, quantity, price, delivery location, job code
  • Approval matrix enforced based on thresholds

Step 2: Receiving Process

  • Receiving department verifies delivery against PO
  • Receiving report documents date, quantity, condition, delivery location
  • Discrepancies reported immediately to purchasing
  • Receiving report forwarded to accounts payable

Step 3: Invoice Processing

  • AP matches: Purchase Order + Receiving Report + Vendor Invoice
  • Verifies quantities, prices, terms, mathematical accuracy
  • Codes invoice to proper GL account and job number
  • Routes to appropriate approver

Month 5 Quiz

Question 1: In a construction chart of accounts, the account "Costs in Excess of Billings" represents: a) Materials purchased but not used b) Work performed but not yet billed c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings d) Equipment costs allocated to projects

Answer: c) Costs and profit earned exceeding customer billings

Explanation: This WIP asset account captures situations where total costs incurred plus gross profit recognized exceed the amount billed to customers, representing earned but unbilled revenue.

Question 2: Calculate the percentage complete and revenue recognition:

  • Contract Value: $1,200,000
  • Costs Incurred: $720,000
  • Total Estimated Costs: $960,000
  • Progress Billings: $800,000

Answer:

  • Percentage Complete: $720,000 ÷ $960,000 = 75%
  • Revenue Earned: $1,200,000 × 75% = $900,000
  • WIP Position: ($720,000 + $180,000) - $800,000 = $100,000 asset

Question 3: Which segregation of duties violation creates the highest fraud risk? a) Same person prepares and signs checks b) Same person receives payments and makes deposits c) Same person approves POs and receives goods d) Same person enters timecards and calculates payroll

Answer: a) Same person prepares and signs checks

Explanation: This eliminates independent verification of payments and allows one person to initiate, approve, and execute transactions without oversight.

Question 4: Equipment depreciation in construction companies should be: a) Always recorded as operating expense b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction c) Recorded only when equipment is sold d) Never allocated to specific projects

Answer: b) Allocated to projects as direct cost when used for construction

Explanation: Construction equipment used on projects should have depreciation allocated as a direct cost to ensure proper job costing and project profitability analysis.

Question 5: The three-way match process includes: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice b) Budget, purchase order, payment c) Invoice, check, bank statement d) Timecard, payroll, tax deposit

Answer: a) Purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice

Explanation: Three-way matching verifies that goods ordered (PO) match goods received (receiving report) and goods invoiced (vendor invoice) before payment authorization.
